keyTakeaways: Shared projection, personal devices, and hybrid delivery create different audience experiences; none is automatically the most accessible choice.
Mobile surtitles can help with touring, difficult sightlines, and individual language choice, but require device, connectivity, communication, support, and fallback planning.
A shared display provides a valuable no-personal-device path, while hybrid delivery can broaden access only when both paths are properly rehearsed.
Multilingual translation and accessibility captions may overlap, but they are not interchangeable audience services.

faq.question: Are mobile surtitles more accessible than projected surtitles?
faq.answer: Not automatically. Mobile surtitles can improve language choice and serve seats without a clear view of a shared screen, but they may exclude patrons without a suitable device, battery, connection, or confidence using the interface. The right choice depends on the audience and venue.

faq.question: When are BYOD mobile surtitles useful?
faq.answer: They can be useful for touring productions, heritage or site-specific venues, variable sightlines, and events that need several language choices. Productions still need to test connectivity and devices, explain phone use, provide staff support, and plan a realistic alternative.

faq.question: What is hybrid surtitle delivery?
faq.answer: Hybrid delivery combines a shared projected or fixed display with an optional audience browser. It can preserve a common, device-free reading path while adding languages or alternative sightlines, provided both paths are prepared and rehearsed.

faq.question: Do translated surtitles provide a complete accessibility service?
faq.answer: No. Translation surtitles help audiences understand dialogue in another language. Accessibility captions may also require speaker identification, meaningful sound information, and editorial decisions shaped by Deaf and hard-of-hearing audiences.

glossary.definition: A projected, LED, or venue-integrated text surface read collectively by the audience.
Prepared performance text opened by patrons on their own browser-enabled phone or tablet, usually through a QR code or link.
A production design that offers both a shared display and a personal-device viewing path.
A tested alternative that preserves a usable audience experience when the preferred display, device, or network path is unavailable.
Same-language text that may identify speakers and meaningful sounds as well as represent spoken dialogue for Deaf and hard-of-hearing audiences.
